Homeostasis and excretion

text: Keeping the inside of you steady.
say: This chapter is really about one big idea: keeping your insides steady.
Homeostasis means keeping your internal environment constant: the same temperature, the same water and salt, whatever is happening outside.
Excretion is getting rid of waste made by your own cells, like urea and carbon dioxide.
Don't mix it up with egestion. That's just getting rid of food you never digested.

text: Narrow exit: efferent narrower than afferent.

say: Your kidneys don't decide on their own how much water to keep. Your brain turns the dial.

text: Short of water: the hypothalamus notices.

text: More ADH: from the pituitary gland.

Inside a kidney

text: Three zones, each with a job.
say: Cut a kidney in half, and you can see three different zones.
The outer layer is the cortex. That's where the filtering happens, in about a million tiny tubes called nephrons.
Inside is the medulla, made of cone-shaped pyramids. The long loops of the nephrons dip down here to save water.
In the middle is the pelvis, a funnel that collects the urine and pours it into the ureter.

The urinary system

text: Two kidneys clean your blood, all day.
say: Your urinary system is small, but it cleans all of your blood many times a day.
Blood arrives at each kidney in the renal artery, gets cleaned, and leaves in the renal vein.
The waste becomes urine, which trickles down two thin tubes, the ureters, to the bladder.

text: Bladder and urethra: store it, then let it out.
say: The bladder stores it until a ring of muscle, the sphincter, relaxes and lets it out through the urethra.
